docs.title: What you get with Docker Desktop
docs.text:
• Docker Engine = Docker service. The main part of Docker that enables virtualizations. It is a server that manages images and containers.
  • Docker Client (CLI): The docker command you run in the terminal. Talks with Docker Engine via the REST API.
  • GUI Client: Also comes with the GUI. These are visual front-ends that also talk to Docker Engine.
  • Docker Registery: storage + distribution system for Docker images.

docs.title: Docker images vs containers
docs.text:
• Image

    • A packaged, read-only template that contains the directories, files, application code, dependencies, runtime, system libraries, and configuration needed to run the application.
    • The image is the artifact that Docker builds.
    • Images do not typically store environment variable values (especially secrets). Those are passed into the container at runtime using .env (docker run -e ENV_NAME=value myimage), docker-compose.yml etc.

  • Container

    • Image -> Container. This is where the image runs. A running instance of an image = container.
    • We take the package/image -> download it to a local laptop/server -> run it -> runs in a container.
    • From the same image we can run multiple containers.
    • Countainers are Ephemeral (can be started, stopped, deleted).
# What images do we have locally?
docker images

# List of running containers
docker ps

# List of all containers running or stopped
# -a or -all = Lists all containers (stopped and running)
docker ps -a

docs.title: Docker registries (e.g., Docker Hub)
docs.text:
• How do we get Docker images? → From a Docker registry.
  • A registry is a storage + distribution system for Docker images.
  • Official/verified images are available.
  • Docker Hub (https://hub.docker.com/) is the biggest registry and the default location Docker checks.
  • You don’t need an account to search/pull public images.
  • Images are versioned using tags (e.g., python:3.11).
  • Special tag: latest = default/most recent build.
  • Best practice: specify a version tag, not latest.
  • !docker run command always creates a new container unless you restart an existing one.
# Download image from Docker hub to run locally
# docker pull name:tag
docker pull nginx:1.23

# Run image as a container
docker run nginx:1.23

# "start worker processes" in the printed logs indicates that the container is running.
# id and name of the container are  assigned.

# Run in detached mode: Runs image as a container in the background without blocking the terminal
# Use -d or --detach flag = detached mode
# Runs container in the background and prints the container id
docker -d run nginx:1.23

# Run commad without pulling..does not have to pull to have locally--can just use run and itll pull for us. Run directly.
docker run nginx:1.22-alpine


# How to see logs now - in detach mode?
docker logs {container-id}
# Like:
docker logs 5d39dfa24f4d

docs.title: Private Docker registries
docs.text:
• Companies may not want images to be public → private registries.
  • AWS ECR = Elastic Container Registeries which provides storage.
  • Docker Hub also supports private registries → create an account and store private/public images.

docs.title: Registry vs repository
docs.text: • Repository: A collection inside a registry for one application. Each app gets its own repository, and inside it you store multiple image versions/tags.

docs.title: Port binding: how do we access this container?
docs.text:
• Containers run inside an isolated Docker network → cannot be accessed from your local machine by default → need port binding.
  • Each app inside a container runs on a specific internal port based on defaults (e.g., 80 for web servers).
  • Port binding maps container port → host port so you can access it from your machine, e.g.: host 9000 → container 80.
  • Example: docker run -p 9000:80 nginx
# Stop 1 or more running containers
docker stop {container}
docker stop 5c8facc9cd21

# Port binding
# Accessible to us at port 9000
# Standard practice to use the same port on the local machine but you can bind to other ports
# host 9000 → container 80
docker run -d -p 9000:80 nginx:1.23

# List of all containers running or stopped
# -a or -all = Lists all containers (stopped and running)
docker ps -a

# Restart a container
docker start {container} #  = Start 1 or more running containers
docker stop 5c8facc9cd21

# Set the name of the container instead of random assignment
# Assign a meanigful container name when we create them
# --name = web-app
docker run --name web-app -d -p 9000:80 nginx:1.23

docs.title: Dockerfile: how to create a Docker image
docs.text:
• Dockerfile → build → Image → Run → Container. Say an application is ready and we want to make it available to users by running it on a server:
  • We need to create a definition of how to build an image from our application. This is written in a Dockerfile
  • Dockerfile is a text document that conatines commands to assemble an image.
  • Docker can then build an image by reading those instructions.
  • Dockerfile starts from a parent image or "base image". Most of these base images are linux based and we build on top of this. These are defined using FROM. FROM is the 1st directive in the Docker file.
  • All directives are written in caps.
  • We map everything we would do to run the application locally inside the container -- write any linux command
  • RUN: Will execute any command in a shell inside the container environment (e.g. installing dependencies). Each RUN creates a new image layer.
  • WORKDIR: Sets the working directory for any following instructions (RUN, COPY, CMD, ...) — similar to cd. Created automatically if it doesn't exist.
  • Next, we need application code → take files from local folder and copy them into the container.
  • COPY <src> <dest>: Copies files/folders from the host into the image. Copying dependency manifests (e.g. package.json) before the rest of the code lets Docker cache the install step on rebuilds.
  • CMD: The default command run when a container starts from this image. Only takes effect once — the last CMD in the file wins. Written in exec form: ["executable", "arg1", "arg2"].

docs.title: Image layers
docs.text:
• An image is a stack of layers, not one solid blob. Most instructions (FROM, RUN, COPY, ADD) each add one new layer on top of the previous ones.
  • Docker caches each layer. On rebuild, if an instruction is unchanged, Docker reuses its cached layer instead of re-running it. The first changed instruction forces that layer, and every layer after it, to rebuild.
FROM python:3.11-slim          # Layer 1: base OS + Python runtime
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./ # Layer 2: adds dependency files
RUN uv sync --frozen           # Layer 3: adds installed packages (.venv)
COPY . .                       # Layer 4: adds the rest of your source
  • Edit main.py and rebuild → layers 1–3 are unchanged, so Docker reuses them from cache. Only layer 4 (COPY . .) reruns — uv sync is skipped.
  • Edit pyproject.toml/uv.lock and rebuild → layer 2 changes, so layers 2, 3, and 4 all rerun — uv sync reinstalls.
  • This is why the full example below copies the dependency files and installs them before copying the rest of the source: it keeps installs cached across source-only changes.
# Start from a base image (name:tag)
FROM python:3.11-slim

# Install uv (dependency manager/resolver)
RUN pip install uv

# Change into this directory inside the container — like `cd`.
# Created automatically if it doesn't exist. Every instruction after
# this (COPY, RUN, CMD, ...) runs relative to /app.
WORKDIR /app

# Copy just the dependency files first (better layer caching:
# if only source code changes, the install step below is skipped
# on rebuilds since Docker caches layers by content).
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./

# Install dependencies into .venv. Runs as a shell command inside
# the container. --frozen = don't update the lockfile, just install
# exactly what's pinned.
RUN uv sync --frozen

# Now copy the rest of the application code
# COPY <src on host> <dest in container>
COPY . .

# Document the port the app listens on (doesn't actually publish
# it — that still needs -p at `docker run`)
EXPOSE 8000

# The command that runs when the container starts.
# Only one CMD per Dockerfile — if there are several, the last wins.
# Exec form (JSON array) is preferred over shell form.
CMD ["uv", "run", "main.py"]

docs.title: Build Docker image from above definition
docs.text:
• docker build -t <name>:<tag> <path> reads the Dockerfile at <path> (. = current dir, i.e. build context) and produces a new image.
  • Rebuilding with the same name:tag doesn't create a second image — it replaces what that tag points to (the old image becomes untagged/"dangling" unless something else still references it).
# Build: -t names/tags the image, . = build context (current dir)
docker build -t my-app:1.0 .

# Confirm it's there
docker images # Should show my-app with tag 1.0

# Run it as a container — host port : container port
docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name my-app-container my-app:1.0

# Check it's actually up
docker ps
docker logs my-app-container
curl localhost:8000

# Rebuild after code changes and rerun
docker build -t my-app:1.0 .
docker stop my-app-container && docker rm my-app-container
docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name my-app-container my-app:1.0

docs.title: Why Docker Compose?
docs.text:
1. Applications are composed of many different parts: APIs, databases, other services, microservice applications.
  2. When creating containerized applications, all these apps must be deployed and run together because they have dependencies on each other.
  3. We have a set of containers running different apps and services in them that need to run together and talk to each other.
  4. Docker Compose allows you to define and run multiple services and apps that belong together in 1 isolated environment → want to deploy multiple docker containers where each container has its own config options, you can use docker compose to manage these containers easily. Useful for multi-container Docker applications.

docs.title: Without Docker Compose
docs.text:
# Need Docker installed and running
# 1) Create Docker Network
# where 2 containers run and talk to each other
docker network create mongo-network
docker network ls

# 2) Start MongoDB container
docker run -d \
-p 27017:27017 \
-e MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME=admin \
-e MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD=supersecret \
--network mongo-network \
--name mongodb \
mongo


# 3) Start Mongo Express Container: UI for Mongo
docker run -d \
-p 8081:8081 \
-e ME_CONFIG_MONGODB_ADMINUSERNAME=admin \
-e ME_CONFIG_MONGODB_ADMINPASSWORD=supersecret \
--network mongo-network \
--name mongo-express \
mongo-express
  • docker compose exec — run a command inside an already-running container (as opposed to docker compose run, which spins up a fresh one).

docs.title: Configuring your Git profile
docs.text:
You need to configure your git client so your commits are attributed to you

# How the current git configuration look like
git config --list

# How the current git configuration look like for a particular repo

git config --list --local

# To view the actual file
cat .git/config

git config --global user.name "Ishita Gopal"
git config --global user.email "xyz@gmail.com"

  • --global: Applies the configuration globally on this computer. Meaning, whenever you make a commit in any Git Repo on your computer, Git will record that commit as being authored by xyz@gmail.com

  • without --global: If you want to set it only for one repository (not globally),

git config user.email "xyz@gmail.com"

docs.title: Set up SSH key-based authentication for GitHub
docs.text:
• This controls how your computer securely connects to GitHub’s servers when you push, pull, or clone code.

  • SSH authentication setup is completely separate from the git config setup which controls how your name and email appear in your commits.

  • You need to create a pair of keys - public and private - and copy the public key into Github. Got to Settings >> SSH and GPG keys >> New SSH Key

# Generate the SSH key pair
ssh-keygen

# Navigate to the SSH directory
cd ~/.ssh

# View (copy) your public key
cat id_rsa.pub

# Add the key to Github and test the connection
ssh -T git@github.com

Note: The test should return: Hi ! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.

docs.text:
Option 1: Make a new dir and then initalize it as a git repo 

mkdir xyz
cd xyz
git init
Option 2: If using uv, it will initalize automatically when you create a project

uv init xyz

Option 3: When contributing to an already existing repo:

docs.title: Typical workflow
docs.text:
1. Make sure you have the latest copy of the repo.
git pull
  1. Tell git which files have changed and should be added in the next snapshot. It is good practice to add a single file at a time.

git add {filename}
 ```

3. Take a snapshot. Good commit messages lead to a usable git log. **If applied this commit will... Eg: "Add a sum function"**
git commit -m "a meaningful but short message describing the changes you made" 
4. Make the snapshot available in the remote repo, so others can see it
git push 
## But before you can push, attach your local repo to GitHub
1. **Eg: Create a new repository called workflows:** Go to GitHub → click New Repository → name it workflows → don’t initialize with README (if you already have a local repo).

2. **Add the remote repository in your local repository:** This uploads your local commits to the remote repository. The remote is named "origin" by convention.
    ```
    git remote add origin https://github.com/username/workflows.git
    ```
3. **Check the remote repository:**
    ```
    git remote -v
    ```
4. **Push the local change:** Takes a copy of my repository and pushes it to GitHub.
    ```
    git push -u origin main
    ```
    - `-u`: link local branch → remote branch (upstream).
    - `origin`: The default nickname for the remote repository. Without it, you’d have to type the full repo URL each time
    - `main`: The branch you’re pushing (In this case, main)

    This creates a tracking relationship:
    - main ↔ origin/main
    - After this, you can just run: `git push` (no need to specify `main`branch again)
    - Every new branch needs the `-u` step once:
    ```
    # 1st time pushing branch
    git push -u origin new-feature

    # After that
    git push
    ```
## Git fetch and pull

`git fetch origin`:
- **Downloads** the latest changes from the remote (e.g. GitHub) into your local repo
- **Does NOT change** your local files
- After fetching, you can inspect changes:
    ```
    git log origin/main
    git diff origin/main
    ```

`git pull`: Fetches and immediately merges/rebases
- **Fetches changes AND merges** them into your current branch. Updates my code immediately.

`git pull --rebase`
1. Fetches changes from the remote
2. Temporarily removes your local commits
3. Applies remote changes first
4. Re-applies your commits on top

## Remove files and directories

Delete a file or director from the repo. Removing files via git allows them to be recovered.
git rm {filename} git rm -r {directory} 
## Get logs
To just get logs or just titles of commit messages
git log git log --oneline git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate 
## Renaming files
git mv OLD NEW 
## Remove remote
git remove origin 
## .gitignore
This file will allow us to tell git which files/directories we don't want to be part of the repo ever. This is useful for keeping credentials, data etc. out of your github repo.


## GitHub flow

- https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hG_P6IRAjNQ


## Merge

- https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0chZFIZLR_0
- https://www.youtube.com/shorts/KiMsYF8fff8



### Merge vs rebase

- **Rebase** = clean linear history, use on your own local/feature branches
- **Merge** = preserves full history, use on shared branches

- **Note**: When you rebase, your local history diverges from the remote, so a normal git push gets rejected. You need to force push to overwrite the remote.

    `--force` → overwrites the remote no matter what

    `--force-with-lease` → overwrites the remote only if no one else has pushed to the branch since your last fetch

docs.title: Before first push — main moves forward:
docs.text: git fetch origin git rebase origin/main git push origin your-feature-branch

docs.title: After first push — main moves forward again:
docs.text: git fetch origin git rebase origin/main git push --force-with-lease origin your-feature-branch

docs.title: If others are working on your branch — main moves forward:
docs.text:
git fetch origin git merge origin/main git push origin your-feature-branch

### Key rules
- ✅ Solo on branch → rebase + force push is fine
- ✅ Use `--force-with-lease` instead of `--force` (safer)
- ❌ Never rebase a branch others are committing on top of
- ⚠️  If others are building on your branch → use merge instead


## Stash
- Stash command is used when you have changes that you are not quite ready to commit.
- You want to revert back (temporarily) to where you started
- You dont know what to do with your changes yet.
- Stash carries over from branch to branch

Stash will save them to a temprary place and you can get back to them later on

```bash
# Save stash with a message
git stash save "Worked on add function"

# All stashes have ids and messages
git stash list

# Takes changes from the stash but does not get rid of the stash
git stash apply stash@{0}

# Grabs the latest stash + applies it + drops the stash
git stash pop

# Get rid of a stash
git stash drop stash@{0}

# Get rid of all stash
git stash clear

Most likely case.. You were on the wrong branch (say, main) and made changes that were supposed to be in another branch.

git checkout main

## made some changs....

# Stash the changes
git stash save "Add function"

# Go to correct branch
git checkout add

# Apply changes
git stash pop

docs.title: Bad/wrong commit message
docs.text:
• Change the message without creating another commit
  • --ammend unique hash is different/changed
  • When the hash changes -> means it chaged the git history. We only want to do this if we are the only ones who have had access to the changes. If we pushed the changes for other users to see, we do not want to change the hsistory because it can cause problems. There are other ways to make corrections without changing the git history. soft: - reset back to the commit we specify + keeps changes in the staging directory

docs.title: git revert : Undo commit but other people have pulled the changes
docs.text:
• You should not change the git history if other peopl have pulled those changes already
  • revert creates new commits to reverse the effect of some earlier commits
  • You dont re write any history. This does not modify or delete the existing commits we have made.
  • It creates new commits on top of the existing commits that comepletely undo all of the changes, so our history remains intact.

# Get hash of the commit you want to undo

# Save exit

# Latest commit shows 'Revert "Commit Message"'

docs.title: Example: pushed commit to the wrong branch
docs.text:
# 1. See what's on the current (wrong) branch and confirm the commit that needs to move
git status
git log --oneline -3

# 2. Fetch to make sure the target branch ref is up to date locally
git fetch origin

# 3. Create a local branch tracking the *correct* remote branch
git checkout -b fix/missing-abstract-csv-322 origin/fix/missing-abstract-csv-322

# 4. Cherry-pick the misplaced commit onto the correct branch
git cherry-pick <commit-sha>

# 4a. If conflicts occur, resolve them in the flagged files, then:
git add <resolved-file>
git cherry-pick --continue
# (git cherry-pick --abort would bail out instead, if needed)

# 5. Push the corrected branch
git push origin fix/missing-abstract-csv-322

# 6. Switch back to the branch that had the mistaken commit
git checkout feat/csv-converter-cli-config

# 7. Revert the commit there (adds a new "revert" commit — does NOT rewrite history)
git revert --no-edit <commit-sha>

# 8. Sanity-check the branch is back to its pre-mistake state
git diff <last-good-commit> HEAD -- <affected-files>   # should be empty

# 9. Push the revert
git push origin feat/csv-converter-cli-config

docs.title: Example: switch to remote branch locally
docs.text:
git fetch origin                    # make sure you have the latest remote refs
git checkout <branch-name>          # e.g. git checkout fix/218-verbatim-text-output
If the branch doesn't exist locally yet, modern git (2.23+) will auto-create a local tracking branch from origin/ as long as the name is unambiguous — so git checkout alone usually just works. That's shorthand for:

git checkout -b <branch-name> origin/<branch-name>

Use the explicit -b ... origin/... form when you want to be unambiguous, or when the short form fails (e.g. name collision with a local branch, or git version too old for the auto-tracking shortcut).

If you're using the newer worktree-style syntax, git switch <branch-name> is the more modern equivalent of git checkout for this purpose. checkout switch git checkout < branch > git switch < branch > git checkout -b < new > git switch -c < new >

docs.title: The core idea
docs.text: An API is just a server sitting somewhere (here: http://127.0.0.1:8000) that accepts requests over HTTP and sends back responses. A client is just the thing making those requests — in our case, a small Python object (httpx.Client, wrapped by destiny_sdk's OAuthClient) that knows the server's address and handles the boring plumbing (auth headers, JSON encoding) for you.

docs.title: The four verbs that matter here
docs.text:
1. GET — "show me what's there." Read-only, doesn't change anything. client.get("/robots//") = "give me this robot's current data."

  2. POST — "create something new." POST /robots/ = "register a brand-new robot," which is why it hands back a new ID + secret.

  3. PUT — "replace this thing entirely with what I'm sending you." PUT /robots// = "here's the complete new state of this robot" — not a patch, the whole object. That's why the GET-then-PUT dance was necessary: you have to fetch the current name/description/owner first, or your PUT would blank them out.

  4. (There's also DELETE, which this API doesn't even expose for robots — hence no way to remove one.) Why GET-then-PUT specifically

    5. Robots don't support partial updates. So the pattern is always: GET the current object → see what's there now. Take that, change the one field you care about (entitlements). PUT the whole thing back.

    client = OAuthClient(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000", auth=httpx.Auth()).get_client()

    After this runs, client is just a variable holding a Python object — think of it like a little assistant that now permanently knows "the server lives at http://127.0.0.1:8000." You don't have to type that address again for every request; you just say client.get(...) or client.put(...) and it fills that part in for you.

    "knows the server's address" — that's just the base_url you gave it. Every call like client.get("/robots/<id>/") gets glued onto that base automatically — you're really hitting http://127.0.0.1:8000/robots/<id>/.

    "auth headers" — every HTTP request can carry extra metadata called headers, and one of them (Authorization) is how you prove who you are. Instead of you manually attaching "hey here's my token" to every single request, the client does it automatically once it's configured — that's the whole point of the auth= argument.

    "JSON encoding" — Python has its own data shapes (dicts, sets, custom objects like RobotIn). The server only understands plain text in a format called JSON. So when we did:

    resp = client.put(f"/robots/{robot_id}/", json=updated.model_dump(mode="json")) model_dump(mode="json") converts our Python object into a JSON-shaped dict, and client.put(..., json=...) turns that into text and sends it. On the way back, .json() (like in current = client.get(...).json()) does the reverse — turns the server's text response back into a normal Python dict you can index with current["name"].

    So the one-sentence version: the client object remembers the address and your credentials so every client.get(...) / client.put(...) call is just "send this data, get data back" — you never have to hand-write the raw HTTP request yourself.

docs.title: curl
docs.text:
curl is a command-line tool that does the exact same thing as client.get(...) in Python, except you type it straight into the terminal — no Python needed at all. It's the fastest way to just poke a URL and see what comes back.

Here's what each one we ran actually did: `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/robots/019fa9ba-2c7c-7777-a341-93c72f1c1d2b/

`

— just print the raw response body to the terminal. This is the plain "show me what this returns" version, equivalent to client.get(...).json() but skipping Python entirely.

docs.title: Class methods
docs.text:
• Regular methods: automatically takes the instance as the first argument (called self by convention).
  • Class methods: automatically takes class as the first argument (called cls by convention).
    • To make a function into a classmethod, we just need to add the @classmethod decorator.
    • Class methods can be used as alternative constructors. By convention, these fuction names start with a 'from' (eg: from_string())
  • Static methods: Don't pass anything automatically (neither instance nor the class).
    • They behave just like regular functions. We use them when there is a logical connection to the class.
    • To make a function into a classmethod, we just add the @staticmethod decorator.
    • If you don't access the instance or class in the method, it likely should be a static method.
# cls is used by convention

class Employee:
    num_of_emps = 0
    raise_amt = 1.04

    def __init__(self, first, last, pay):
        self.first = first
        self.last = last
        self.pay = pay

    def fullname(self):
        return '{} {}'.format(self.first, self.last)

    # Set class variable 
    @classmethod
    def set_raise_amt(cls, amount): 
        cls.raise_amt = amount 

    # ALternative constructor
    @classmethod
    def from_string(cls, emp_str):
        first, last, pay = emp_str.split('-')
        return cls(first, last, pay)

    # Static method 
    # Return if its a workday
    @staticmethod
    def is_workday(day):
        if day.weekday == 5 or day.weekday == 6:
            return False
        return True

# Class method example
# Working with the class instead of the instance
Employee.set_raise_amt(1.05)

# Alternative constructors 
emp_str_1 = 'John-Doe-70000'
new_emp_1 = Employee.from_string(emp_str_1)

# Static method example 
my_date = datetime.date(2016, 7, 11)
Employee.is_workday(my_date)

Pathlib has limited ability to create, move, and delete files/dirs.

p.rmdir()  # delete dir — only works on EMPTY directories

docs.title: Pydantic
docs.text:
• Used in data processing for ensuring clean data
  • Used by Fast API

docs.title: Type hints vs type checking vs data validation
docs.text:
1. Type Hints: A way to annotate variables, function parameters, and return values with expected types. This does not enforce types at runtime; it’s purely informational.

  2. Type Checking: Detect type errors before runtime using tools like mypy. This does static analysis; no runtime effect unless combined with runtime checks.

  3. Data Validation: Actively checks that data meets certain criteria (types, ranges, formats, constraints) at runtime. It enforce correctness at runtime.

docs.title: Create a simple user model
docs.text:
• Gives the benefit of a nice syntax with type hints + data validation at runtime
  • Collects all validation error at once
  • The username and email is required
  • bio and is_active are optional fields with defaults
  • full_name can be a string or None and default is None (| = union)
# uv add pydantic
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError
from datetime import datetime

class User(BaseModel):
    uid: int
    username: str
    email: str

    verified_at: datetime | None = None

    bio: str = ""
    is_active:bool = True
    full_name: str | None = None

docs.title: Accessing and modifying data
docs.text:
• You can access fields using dot notation.
  • Model instances are mutable by default.
  • Models do not revalidate when you change a field. 
user = User(uid=123,
            username = "igopal",
            email = "igopal@gmail.com")

print(user.username) # prints igopal

user.bio = 123 # Will run fine. Is not revalidating on assignment

docs.title: Model to dictionary
docs.text:
Useful for: - serializing: converting to a simpler format for storage and sharing or sending over a network

user.model.dump() # python dictionary

user.model.dump_json(indent=2) # json

docs.title: Handling validation errors
docs.text: • Some type coercion is enabled by default in pydantic. Pydantic will try to convert types when it makes sense to do so. '123' --> 123 automatically

docs.title: Different types
docs.text:
• Supports all standard python types
  • We can use unions, optionals, literal types
  • Below we set a list of tags with defaults
    • default_factory: function that is called to create a default each time you create an instance. Creates an empty list for each instance.
    • We use a lamda function for datetime to return an unexecuted function that should run each time an instance is created
    • partial() is the alternative to the lambda function.
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Literal
from datetime import datetime

class BlogPost(BaseModel):
    titles: str
    content: str
    view_count: int = 0
    is_published: bool =False

    # Set list as default
    tags: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)  

    # Pass an unexecuted function using lambda
    create_at: datetime = Field(default_factory = lambda: datetime.now(tz=UTC))
    # Another way to do the same thing
    create_at: datetime = Field(default_factory = partial(datetime.now, tz=UTC))

    # Union type 
    author_id: str | int 

    # Literal types 
    status: Literal["draft", "published", "archived"] = "draft"

docs.title: Using Field and Annotated
docs.text:
• Can be used to set defaults
  • Add constraints, like, min, max, patterns, linked requirements. The reccomended way to do this is to use Annotated type form Typing
  • Annotated adds metadata to our current type. For uid, we say: we want an integer but with the metadata that the value is greater than 0.
  • Pydantic has shorthand of constraints built in : (ref:
  • https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/types/#pydantic.types.NonPositiveInt

  • https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/networks/)

  • Some of these will have dependencies. Eg:, EmailStr requires the email validator library. (Do uv add pydantic[email] in terminal. []=optional dependencies) 

    from typing import Annotated, Literal 
from datetime import datetime
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, EmailStr, HttpUrl, SecretStr, ValidationError
from uuid import UUID, uuid4

class User(BaseModel):
    # int that is greater than 0
    uid: Annotated[int, Field(gt=0)]

    # Min and max length 
    username: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=3, max_length=20)]

    # age is where ge (or greater than or =) 13 and  le(less than or equal) <=130
    age: Annotated[int, Field(ge=13, le=130)]

    # Using regular expression pattern:
    #  should only contain lower case letters, numbers and hyphens
    slug: Annotated[str, Field(pattern="^[a-z0-9-]+$")]


class User(BaseModel):

    # Make it uid with a default factory that generates a unique id -- autogenerated
    uid: UUID = Field(default_factory=uuid4)

    username: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=3, max_length=20)]

    # Change email to email string 
    email: EmailStr

    # User Website
    website: HttpUrl | None = None

    # Password --- it will hide the password when you print out the model ****
    password: SecretStr

# To access the password value 
user = User (username = "..", email=..., age =39, password ='secret123')
user.password.get_secret_value()

docs.title: Custom validators
docs.text:
• Sometimes the built constraints in validation are not enough, and you may want to add your own logic.
  • We can easily do this in Pydantic with decorators.
  • After validation
    • Default
    • Runs after pydantic has already done its typechecking and basic validation
    • Ex below: validate_username
  • Before validation
    • Used when you want to preprocess data before the main validation happens.

docs.title: @field_validator
docs.text:
• In the example, validate_username:
    • We valdate that username only contain alphanumeric characters and underscores + normalize them to lowercase
    • This is an after validation
  • In the example, add_https:
    • This is an example of before validation
    • We do some preprocessing and run some custom validation and modification for the website before it does the HttpUrl validation above
    • It checks if the website start with http:// or https://. If not, it adds it to the beginning.
    • Then the HttpUrl validation runs 
from uuid import UUID, uuid4
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import (
    BaseModel, 
    Field, 
    EmailStr, 
    HttpUrl, 
    SecretStr, 
    ValidationError,
    field_validator, 
    model_validator, 
    ValidationError
    )

class User(BaseModel):
    uid: UUID = Field(default_factory=uuid4)
    username: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=3, max_length=20)] 
    password: SecretStr
    website: HttpUrl | None = None
    age: Annotated[int, Field(ge=13, le=130)]

    # Pass in the field we are validating : username
    @field_validator("username")
    @classmethod
    def validate_username(cls, v: str) -> str:
        if not v.replace("_", "").isalnum():
            raise ValueError("Username must be alphanumeric (underscores allowed)"
        return v.lower()

    # Mode = "before"
    @field_validator("website", mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def add_https(cls, v: str | None) -> str | None:
        if v and not v.startswith(("http://", "https://")):
            return f"https://{v}"
    return v 


# Website validation 

User (
    username = .. 
    email=..., 
    age =39, 
    password ='secret123',
    website = 'coreyms.com') # this will give an error if mode it not set to before because the website string does not start with http or https

docs.title: @model_validator
docs.text:
• Useful when you want to validate multiple fields together or when you want to validate the complete model. EX: Confirming if the password and confir password fields match.
  • Instead of receiving athe value, it receives self = whole model instance. This allows you to access all the fields to do validation.
  • This runs after all the fields have been validated individually. This is why we do not usee @classmethod.
class USerRegistration(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr
    password: str
    confirm_password: str

    @model_validator(mode="after"):
    def passwords_match(self) -> "UserRegistration":
        if self.password != self.confirm_password:
            raise ValueError("Passwords do not match")
        raise self

docs.title: Best practices for validators
docs.text:
• Always return the values even if you are not modeifying it or raise an error
  • You usually want to raise a ValueError for validation errors. - Pydantic converts it into a ValidationError automatially.
  • If you are going to raise an error, don't mutate the value first. Either return the modified value or raise an error, but not both.

docs.title: Computed fields
docs.text:
• Used when you want fields that are calculated/computed from other fields and you want them to be included when you serialize the model to a dictionary or json
  • Use a decorator @computed_field.
  • We can combine it with the @property decorator.
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import (
    BaseModel, 
    Field, 
    EmailStr,
    HttpUrl, 
    SecretStr, 
    computed_field
)

class User(BaseModel):
    username: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=3, max_length=20)]
    password: SecretStr
    website: HttpUrl | None = None
    first_name: str = "" 
    last_name: str = "" 
    follower_count: int = 0

    # Now this will be included when we serialize out model
    @computed_field 
    @property
    def display_name(self) -> str:
        if self.first_name and self.last_name:
            return f"{self.first_name} {self.last_name}"
        return self.username

    @computed_field 
    @property
    def is_influencer(self) -> bool:
        return self.follower_count >= 10000

docs.title: Nested models
docs.text:
• You can use other Pydantic models as field types, i.e., you can have models within models.
  • Pydantic will automatically validate everything recursively
class Comment(BaseModel):
    content: str
    another_email: EmailStr
    likes: int = 0


class BlogPost(BaseModel):
    title: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=10, max_length=200)]
    content: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=10)]
    author_id: str | int

docs.title: What if we wanted to store the full author information instead of just the author id?
docs.text:
• We can use the User model as the type
  • Below we replace author_id with author and set the type as User. So data will have to pass the User validation checks.
  • The full User object will be nested in the blogpost.
  • We can also set the comment that we created above. So the each comment will need to pass the Comment validation checks. 
class BlogPost(BaseModel):
    title: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=10, max_length=200)]
    content: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=10)]
    author: User

    # List of Comment 
    comments: list[Comment] = Field(default_factory=list)

post_data = {
    "title":
    "content":
    "author":{
        "username": "coreyms",
        "age": 39,
        "password": "secret1234"
    }
    "comments":[
        {
            "content": "I think I understand nested models now!",
            "author_email": "student@xyz.com",
            "likes": 25
        },
        {
            "content": "Can you cover FastAPI next?",
            "author_email": "viewer123@example.com",
            "likes": 15
        }
    ]
}

# Creating a blogpost from the post_data:
# Unpacking the dictionary with ** and validating recursively
post = BlogPost(**post_data) 

# Same as using model_validate()
BlogPost.model_validate(post_data)

docs.title: Advanced serialization and working with JSON
docs.text:
• Working with APIs
    • External the external representation may use different field names form internal Python names
    • You may not want some fields serialized
    • Maybe you have some internal fields that you dont want exposed when serialized. -> ConfigDict
    • Allows you do configure our model further
    • populate_by_name: tells pydantic to accept both a fieldname and an alias when loading daa
      • accept id not just uid
      • We dont have to change the whole model. Alias allows us to be a litle more flexible when loading/exporting data.

docs.title: ConfigDict
docs.text:
from pydantic import ConfigDict

class User(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(populate_by_name=True)

    # This will accept data not just with uid but also if the field is named id

    uid: UUID = Field(alias="id", default_factory=uuid4)
    username: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=3, max_length=20)]
    password: SecretStr
    website: HttpUrl | None = None
    first_name: str = "" 
    last_name: str = "" 
    follower_count: int = 0

    # Now this will be included when we serialize out model
    @computed_field 
    @property
    def display_name(self) -> str:
        if self.first_name and self.last_name:
            return f"{self.first_name} {self.last_name}"
        return self.username

    @computed_field 
    @property
    def is_influencer(self) -> bool:
        return self.follower_count >= 10000


user_data = {
    "id":"3bc4567...",
    "username":"corey_shaffer",
    "age":"39",
}

# Will still display as "uid" not "id"
user = User.model_validate(user_data)
print(user.model_dump_json(indent=2))

# Instead of "uid" we will get "id"
print(user.model_dump_json(indent=2, by_alias=True))

# Exclude the password 
print(user.model_dump_json(indent=2, by_alias=True, exclude={"password"}))

# Include only specific fields 
print(user.model_dump_json(indent=2, by_alias=True, include={"username", "email"}))

# Load from json data or a json file 
User.model_validate_json(json_data)

docs.title: Other ConfigDict options
docs.text:
# Controling type coersion and making it strict mode Be very specific about type 
class User(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(
        populate_by_name=True, 
        strict=True
    )
    ...
    ...
    ...

# Handle extra fields 
# By default 
# Allows extra fields 
class User(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(
        populate_by_name=True, 
        strict=True,
        extra = "allow"
    )
    ...
    ...

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
Here’s a simple 10-rule summary you can keep in mind when naming things in Python.

  1. Use snake_case for files, variables, and functions Example: load_data.py, publication_year, filter_papers().

  2. Use PascalCase for classes Example: ClimateHealthClassifier, NetworkAnalyzer.

  3. Use UPPER_CASE for constants Example: CITY_KEYWORDS, YEAR_MIN, REL_THRESHOLD.

  4. Name functions with verbs (actions) Example: load_data(), filter_papers(), compute_metrics().

  5. Name variables with nouns (things/data) Example: papers_df, author_network, publication_year.

  6. Use descriptive names instead of abbreviations Prefer mortality_impacts_df over mort_imp_df.

  7. Keep names consistent across the project Example: always use _df for DataFrames, _path for file paths.

  8. Use prefixes for booleans Example: is_valid, has_location, contains_keyword.

  9. Avoid unnecessary words Prefer climate_health_df over climate_health_dataframe_object.

  10. Make names readable like natural language Code should read clearly: filtered_df = filter_climate_health_papers(papers_df).

One mental test: If someone reads your code aloud and it sounds like a sentence, your naming is probably good.

docs.title: Grep command
docs.text:
• Global regular expression print
  • Allows us to search for text within files on our system
  • When there are no results , it just jumps to the next line

Example, seach a if 'Jane Williams' is within a file

grep 'Jane Williams' names.txt

#  Only return whole words (dont return Jane Williamson)
grep -w "Jane William" names.txt

# Make it cases insenstive
grep -wi "Jane William" names.txt

# Get line info
grep -win "Jane William" names.txt
  • See a certain number of lines before the match
# Returns 4 lines before the match
grep -win -B 4 "Jane William" names.txt

# Returns 4 lines after the match
grep -win -A 4 "Jane William" names.txt

# Returns 2 lines before and after the match = context
grep -win -C 2 "Jane William" names.txt
  • Searching in all files in the current directory
grep -win -A 4 "Jane William" ./*

# Only in the text files
grep -win -A 4 "Jane William" ./*.txt

# search in every single file and subdirectories
grep -winr -A 4 "Jane William" ./

  • Only return the files with matches, not the matches themselves 

    grep - wirl -A 4 "Jane William" .

  • Number of matches in each file

grep -wirc "Jane William"

• Allows you to transfer and sync files efficiently across directories and machines

  • Only syncs files that are different

  • Mirror the source directory and delete anything extra that is in the Backup/ that is not in the Orignal/
